stem: After head trauma, a client briefly loses consciousness, becomes alert, and then rapidly deteriorates neurologically. Which injury is classically associated with this lucid-interval pattern?

options.A: Uncomplicated concussion without an expanding intracranial mass lesion.
options.B: Acute subdural hematoma from torn bridging veins.
options.C: Epidural hematoma, often associated with traumatic middle meningeal arterial bleeding.
options.D: Diffuse axonal injury with immediate widespread traumatic axonal damage.

rationale: NCBI StatPearls describes the classic epidural-hematoma presentation as initial loss of consciousness after trauma, a transient lucid interval, and subsequent rapid neurologic deterioration. Most epidural hematomas are arterial, commonly involving a branch of the middle meningeal artery after skull trauma. The lucid interval is not present in every epidural hematoma and is not pathognomonic, but among these options it is classically associated with epidural hematoma. Acute subdural hematoma more often reflects bridging-vein injury and a more gradual decline, while uncomplicated concussion and diffuse axonal injury do not best match this classic sequence.
educational_objective: Recognize a traumatic loss of consciousness followed by a lucid interval and rapid neurologic decline as the classic warning pattern for epidural hematoma, while remembering that the pattern is not universal or pathognomonic.
source_organization: National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI Bookshelf)
source_version_date: Last update July 7, 2025; StatPearls 2026 edition; accessed 2026-08-16
source_locator: Continuing Education Activity — arterial bleeding/middle meningeal artery and lucid interval; Pathophysiology — middle meningeal arterial source; History and Physical — initial loss of consciousness, lucid interval, rapid neurologic deterioration; Differential Diagnosis — comparison with subdural hematoma
source_claim_supported: Epidural hematoma is classically associated with traumatic loss of consciousness, a lucid interval, and subsequent rapid neurologic decline; bleeding is commonly arterial from the middle meningeal artery, although the lucid interval is not universal or pathognomonic.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)

blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — epidural hematoma recognition after head trauma

source_original.stem: After head trauma, a client briefly loses consciousness, becomes alert, then rapidly deteriorates neurologically. Which injury is classically associated with this lucid-interval pattern?

options.A: Uncomplicated concussion, because rapid deterioration after a lucid interval is expected and benign
options.B: Chronic subdural hematoma, which always produces the same brief lucid interval after a head injury
options.C: Epidural hematoma, often involving traumatic injury to the middle meningeal artery after skull trauma
options.D: Ischemic stroke, because a traumatic lucid interval specifically indicates cerebral arterial embolism

source_original.rationale: A lucid interval after traumatic loss of consciousness followed by neurologic deterioration is classically associated with epidural hematoma, often from middle meningeal arterial injury. The pattern is not present in every epidural hematoma and is not pathognomonic.
source_original.source_detail: History and Physical: classic lucid interval; etiology commonly middle meningeal artery after blunt trauma; last update July 7, 2025; accessed 2026-08-14.

correction_summary: Retained the classic epidural-hematoma construct, replaced obviously false mechanism-heavy distractors with realistic intracranial-injury alternatives, explicitly preserved the nonpathognomonic limitation, and reduced difficulty from hard to easy because the final task is classic pattern recognition.

audit_findings.source_authority: Current NCBI StatPearls; NCSBN 2026 Test Plan
audit_findings.currentness: NCBI chapter updated 2025-07-07 and published in StatPearls 2026 edition.
audit_findings.claim_audit: History and Physical directly supports the loss-of-consciousness/lucid-interval/rapid-decline pattern and explicitly states it is not pathognomonic; Pathophysiology supports the common middle meningeal arterial source.

distractor_audit.A: An uncomplicated concussion does not best explain an expanding-mass pattern with rapid neurologic decline after a lucid interval.
distractor_audit.B: Subdural hematoma is a real post-traumatic differential but more commonly arises from bridging veins and has a more gradual decline than the classic EDH sequence.
distractor_audit.D: Diffuse axonal injury generally causes immediate severe neurologic impairment rather than the classic lucid-interval sequence.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: The source notes lucid intervals may occur in other expanding intracranial lesions; the stem therefore asks 'classically associated,' making C the uniquely best answer rather than claiming pathognomonicity.
audit_findings.cueing: All alternatives are plausible traumatic neurologic diagnoses without fabricated mechanisms in the option text.
audit_findings.blueprint: Physiological Adaptation is appropriate for acute traumatic neurologic deterioration.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Re-read the July 2025 NCBI History/Physical, Pathophysiology, and Differential Diagnosis sections; challenged subdural hematoma as a potential second answer and preserved 'classically associated' plus the nonpathognomonic limitation. C remained uniquely best.
